prompt.context: You have been retained jointly by Pampers and a federal commission on waste management.
prompt.question: Estimate the volume percentage of disposable diapers in the total US household garbage.

framework: Define the ratio: Volume percentage = Volume of disposable diapers discarded per day / Total volume of US household garbage per day
Estimate the numerator: total diaper volume per day (population → diaper-wearing children → diapers per child per day → volume per diaper)
Estimate the denominator: total household garbage volume per day (population → garbage per household per day → total volume)
Compute the ratio and sanity-check the result
Sensitivity: explain how changes in key assumptions would shift the estimate

questions.prompt: Estimate the total volume of disposable diapers thrown away per day in the US.
questions.guidance: Candidate should build up from US population, identify the fraction of diaper-wearing children (~10%), estimate diapers used per child per day (~4), and assign a reasonable volume per diaper (~500 mL). Multiplying through gives total diaper volume per day.

math.setup: Volume of diapers/day = (US population) × (% diaper-wearing children) × (diapers/child/day) × (volume/diaper)
steps: Diapers per child per day = 4 → 120 million diapers/day
Total = 500 mL × 120,000,000 = 60,000,000,000 mL = 60,000,000 liters = 60 million liters/day
math.answer: ~60 million liters of diapers discarded per day

questions.prompt: Estimate the total volume of US household garbage per day.
questions.guidance: Candidate should estimate average garbage volume per household or per person per day. One approach: use population directly with an average daily garbage volume per person (e.g., one 10-liter bag per person per day).

math.setup: Total garbage/day = (US population) × (average garbage volume per person per day)
steps: Average garbage volume per person/day ≈ 10 liters (one standard trash bag)
math.answer: ~3,000 million liters of household garbage per day

questions.prompt: Compute the volume percentage of disposable diapers in total US household garbage.
questions.guidance: Candidate divides diaper volume by total garbage volume and expresses as a percentage.

brainstorming.prompt: How would changes in your key assumptions affect the estimate, and what factors could cause the true figure to be higher or lower?

categories.name: Assumptions that could raise the estimate
ideas: Higher diaper count per day (some sources cite 6–8 for newborns)
Larger diaper volume for overnight/adult diapers
Lower per-person garbage volume (e.g., dense urban households with smaller bags)

categories.name: Assumptions that could lower the estimate
ideas: Lower fraction of diaper-wearing children if birth rates are declining
Thinner/compressed modern diapers reducing volume per unit
Higher average household garbage volume if large families or commercial waste is included

categories.name: Structural factors
ideas: Not all disposable diapers end up in household garbage (some disposed at daycare or public facilities)
Recycling or composting programs for diapers could reduce the household share
Regional variation in birth rates and diaper usage patterns

recommendation: Disposable diapers represent approximately 2% of total US household garbage by volume, based on reasonable assumptions about population, diaper usage rates, and average garbage generation.
This figure is sensitive to the volume-per-diaper assumption and the per-person garbage baseline; the plausible range is roughly 1%–4%.
risks: If diapers are thicker or used more frequently than assumed, the percentage could be materially higher.
The estimate counts only household disposal; institutional disposal (daycares, hospitals) is excluded.
next_steps: Validate volume-per-diaper assumption with product specifications from Pampers.
Refine the per-person household garbage estimate using EPA solid waste data.
Assess implications for landfill capacity and policy recommendations for the federal commission.
